# Signature Chains

A user's set of keys changes over time. Devices are added and revoked, shared
keys are rotated, usernames change. A team's roster changes in the same way,
and so does the set of keys a server uses to sign its own statements. FOKS
records each of these histories as a *signature chain*: an ordered list of
signed entries in which each entry names the one before it. This chapter
explains the general technique, the exact contents of a FOKS link, how links
are bound to the Merkle tree described in [Chapter 11](11-merkle-tree.qmd),
and what the server and the client each check.

## The problem

The server stores the history and hands it to clients on request. The client
must reconstruct the *current* key state from that history and must be able
to tell if the server edited an entry, reordered entries, dropped the most
recent ones, or served one client a different history than another. The
server cannot forge entries, because it does not hold the signing keys, but
without further structure it could freely omit, reorder, and replay them.

## Hash chains and append-only logs

The general technique is old. Haber and Stornetta's 1991 time-stamping scheme
links each document certificate to the previous one by including its hash, so
that altering any certificate changes every later one. Git commits, blockchain
blocks, and Keybase sigchains are all instances of the same idea: an entry
contains the hash of its predecessor, so the whole history up to any entry is
committed by that entry's hash. Add a signature over each entry and the chain
also records *who* appended it.

A hash chain with a signature on each link gives three properties:

- **Integrity.** Changing link $n$ changes its hash, which no longer matches
  the `previous` field of link $n+1$.
- **Order.** Each link states its own sequence number and the hash of the
  link before it, so links cannot be reordered without breaking the chain.
- **Authorship.** Each link is signed by a key that the chain itself, up to
  that point, has authorized.

What a hash chain does not give is protection against *truncation* (serving
the chain up to link $n$ and pretending $n+1$ does not exist) or against
*forking* (serving two different link $n+1$s to two different clients). Those
need an external, published commitment to the chain's current tail, which is
what the Merkle tree provides.

## What a FOKS link contains

A user or team link is carried in an outer envelope that separates the signed
content from the signatures over it:

```
LinkOuter = [ 1, { "1": [ Binary(inner), [ signature, ... ] ] } ]
```

The `inner` bytes are the canonical encoding of the link's content and are
kept verbatim, as [Chapter 9](09-canonical-encoding.qmd) explained. The
link's hash, which is what goes into the Merkle tree, is
$\mathrm{prefixed\_hash}(\texttt{LINK\_OUTER\_TYPE\_ID}, \text{outer bytes})$.
Every link's inner content carries these fields:

| Field                       | Meaning                                                   |
|-----------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| `seqno`                     | position in the chain, starting at 1                      |
| `previous`                  | hash of the prior link; absent only when `seqno` is 1     |
| `root`                      | the Merkle root `{epoch, hash}` the signer observed        |
| `time`                      | the signer's clock, in milliseconds                       |
| `next_location_commitment`  | a commitment to where the *next* link will sit in the tree |
| entity and host             | the user or team ID, and the host it lives on              |
| `signer`                    | the key that made the last signature                      |
| payload                     | member changes, shared-key generations, metadata          |

The `root` field is a *cross-link* from the chain into the tree, and the
`next_location_commitment` is the reverse; both are discussed below. The
payload's metadata items are commitments rather than plaintext: a username
and a device name each appear as an HMAC over the name with a random 16-byte
key, and the key is disclosed only to readers entitled to it.

## Chain types

FOKS keeps several kinds of chain, and each has a numeric *chain type* that
becomes part of its tree keys.

| Chain                    | Chain type | Entity                                   | Notes                                         |
|--------------------------|-----------:|------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| User chain               | 0          | user ID                                  | devices, PUK generations, username metadata   |
| Username ownership       | 1          | `0x09` ‖ hash of `[name, host]`          | one leaf per ownership sequence               |
| User settings subchain   | 2          | user ID                                  | passphrase generation and salt                |
| Team chain               | 3          | team ID                                  | roster, PTK generations, team metadata        |
| Team membership subchain | 4          | user ID                                  | which teams the user has joined or requested  |
| Hostchain                | —          | host ID                                  | the host's own keys; separate encoding        |

The user and team chains are the *main* chains. The settings and membership
chains are *generic subchains*: they use the same outer envelope and the same
`previous`/`root`/`next_location_commitment` fields, carry exactly one
signature each, and differ from the main chains in how their first tree
location is chosen. The username chain is not a signature chain at all; it is
a sequence of tree leaves that record who owns a name, discussed in
[Chapter 11](11-merkle-tree.qmd).

The hostchain has its own envelope, `[1, {"1": [Binary(inner), [signatures]]}]`
hashed under `HOSTCHAIN_LINK_OUTER_TYPE_ID`. Its inner content is a
`chainer {seqno, previous, root, time}`, the host ID, the signer, and a list
of changes, each of which adds a key, revokes a key, or adds a TLS
certificate authority. Host keys are typed: the host's identity key, a
delegated Merkle-signer key, a delegated metadata-signer key, and a TLS CA
key are distinct entity types, and a change item names which one it
introduces. Two hostchain rules are worth stating. The genesis link must be
signed by the host's identity key, which is also the host ID. A revoked
*hostchain-signing* key can never be reintroduced, but revoked delegated keys
can be, because the Go implementation permits it.

## Stacked signatures

Some links need the consent of more than one key. A user's first link is
signed by the new per-user key (PUK), optionally by a hardware-backed subkey,
and by the device that created the account. A link that rotates a shared key
is signed by the new key, to prove possession, and by the device making the
change. A hostchain link is signed by every key it introduces and then by the
signer.

FOKS does not sign the inner bytes once per key. Signature $i$ is computed
over the encoding of `[Binary(inner), [signature_0, …, signature_{i−1}]]`,
with the empty prefix encoded as `Null` because Snowpack has no empty arrays.
Each signer thus signs the inner content *and every signature before it*.
The stack is ordered, and the order is authenticated: swapping two
signatures invalidates both. The verifier replays the stack in the order the
policy dictates. For a user transition the order is: rotated shared keys,
then the provisioning subkey if any and the added device, then the signing
device. For a
hostchain link: introduced keys in the order of the change list, then the
signer. A wrong count of signatures is fatal.

One detail of the ECDSA path is instructive. Signatures from a YubiKey's
P-256 key may be produced with either of the two valid $s$ values, because
the hardware does not normalize them, and the verifier accepts both. The
code comments that replay protection "relies on chain sequence, previous
hash, and Merkle root bindings rather than signature malleability
resistance." Signature malleability would matter if the signature bytes were
the identity of a link; they are not, because the link's identity is the hash
of its outer bytes, and a link with different signature bytes is a different
link with the same `previous`, which the chain rejects.

## Tree-location commitments

A link must be found in the Merkle tree, so it needs a tree key. The obvious
key, a hash of the user ID and sequence number, would let anyone who knows a
user ID enumerate that user's history by probing the tree. FOKS instead
derives the key of link $n$ from a random *tree location* that link $n-1$
committed to:

```
  link n-1                         link n
  +-----------------------------+   +-----------------------------+
  | seqno = n-1                 |   | seqno = n                   |
  | next_location_commitment =  |   | previous = H(link n-1)      |
  |   H(TREE_LOCATION, L_n)  ---+-->| key = H(RF_INPUT,           |
  |                             |   |   [type, entity, n, L_n])   |
  +-----------------------------+   +-----------------------------+
                                       L_n is disclosed alongside link n
```

The signer of link $n-1$ picks 32 random bytes $L_n$ and puts
$\mathrm{prefixed\_hash}(\texttt{TREE\_LOCATION\_TYPE\_ID}, \mathrm{Binary}(L_n))$
into the link. $L_n$ itself is not in the signed link; the server discloses it
in the chain response next to link $n$. The key under which link $n$ is
stored is

$$
\mathrm{prefixed\_hash}(\texttt{MERKLE\_TREE\_RF\_INPUT\_TYPE\_ID},
  [\,\text{chain type},\ \text{entity ID},\ n,\ L_n\,]).
$$

Link 1 of a main chain has no predecessor and uses `Null` in place of the
location. The verifier checks each disclosed location against the previous
link's commitment before deriving the key, so a server cannot move a link to
a key of its own choosing. And because $L_{n+1}$ is fixed by link $n$, the
client can compute the key of the *next* link from state it has already
verified, which is what makes the absence proofs of
[Chapter 11](11-merkle-tree.qmd) meaningful.

## Subchain start locations

Generic subchains hide even their first link. The eldest link of a user or
team carries, in its metadata, a commitment to a 32-byte *seed*. The first
tree location of each subchain is derived from that seed by a keyed hash:

$$
L_1 = \mathrm{HMAC\text{-}SHA\text{-}512/256}\big(\text{seed},\
  \mathrm{BE64}(\texttt{CHAIN\_LOCATION\_DERIVATION\_TYPE\_ID}) \,\|\,
  \mathrm{encode}([\,\text{chain type},\ \{\}\,])\big).
$$

The second element of the array is an empty variant, present for
compatibility with the Go encoding. The seed is disclosed in the subchain
response to readers entitled to it, and the client checks two things before
using it: that the seed's commitment matches the one in the owner's eldest
link, and that the derived location matches where the server actually placed
link 1. The derivation is pinned by a test vector shared with the Go oracle: a
seed of 32 `0x35` bytes and the team-membership chain type derive to the
location beginning `90de9044fcee5b28…`. Later subchain links use ordinary
next-location commitments.

The effect is that a party who knows only a user ID cannot compute any tree
key of that user's settings or membership chains, and cannot compute the key
of any main-chain link after the first without the disclosed locations. The
tree is public; the map from identities to positions in it is not. This is
the same unlinkability goal that CONIKS achieves with a verifiable random
function over the username; FOKS uses commit-then-reveal and a keyed hash
instead.

## What the server checks

The server accepts a link only inside a single database transaction that
also mints the Merkle epoch containing it. Before it does, it checks the
link's `seqno` and `previous` against the stored chain, verifies the
signature stack against the keys the chain has authorized, and validates the
`root` field. That last check, `require_cited_root`, demands that a root at
the cited epoch exists in the server's own root table and that its hash
matches. A companion check notices when a link was built against a
chain head that has since been superseded, so that a client racing with
itself gets a retryable error rather than a fork. The server also re-derives
the subchain start location from the disclosed seed when a subchain's first
link arrives.

## What the client checks

The client's verifier, in `foks-verify`, takes the raw response bytes and an
already-authenticated set of Merkle roots (how those roots become
authenticated is [Chapter 12](12-epochs.qmd)). For a full user-chain load it
proceeds as follows.

1. The root the response was built against must be an authenticated root
   whose epoch is not older than the client's latest, and byte-identical to
   it if the epochs are equal.
2. Every username and device-name commitment in the links must be opened by
   a disclosed `(name, sequence, key)` triple whose HMAC reproduces it.
3. The username's ownership leaves in the tree must show the name belongs to
   this user and to no later claimant.
4. For each link $n$: `seqno` is $n$, `previous` is the hash of link $n-1$,
   the entity and host match, the cited root is in the authenticated set,
   the disclosed location matches the prior link's commitment, and a Merkle
   proof places the link's hash at the derived key under the response root.
5. The eldest link carries two or three stacked signatures in the required
   order, and the user ID equals the PUK verification key re-typed as a user
   ID, so that the identity is self-certifying.
6. Every later link is fed to a replay state machine that enforces policy:
   at most one member change per link, the signer must be an active device,
   shared-key generations only increase, and an owner device must always
   remain.
7. After the last link, the key of link $n+1$, computed from the last
   disclosed location, must be proven *absent* under the response root.

Step 7 is what defeats truncation. The server cannot present links $1..n$ and
stop, because it must also prove that the place where link $n+1$ would go is
empty, and it cannot produce that proof if link $n+1$ exists. Incremental
loads replay only a suffix but still demand that the first disclosed location
match the pinned commitment, that `previous` match the pinned tail hash, and
that the same terminal absence proof be present. The team chain verifier
follows the same skeleton with team-specific policy, and the generic subchain
verifier in the client crate checks continuity, one signature per link, and
the seed-derived start location.

## The mutual binding between chains and roots

Three commitments run in a cycle, and every arrow is verified:

```
   hostchain tail  <------ cited by ------  Merkle root
        |                                      ^
        | authorizes the                       | leaves are
        | Merkle-signer key                    | link hashes
        v                                      |
   signature on root  ---- covers -------->  chain links ---- cite ----> Merkle root
```

- The Merkle root names the hostchain tail `{seqno, hash}` at the time it was
  minted. A verifier requires that tail to equal the tail of the hostchain it
  has verified, and requires the root's signature to come from a Merkle-signer
  key that hostchain currently authorizes.
- The root's leaves are hashes of chain links, so a root commits to the
  contents of every chain.
- Each chain link cites the root its signer saw. The verifier requires that
  cited root to be an authenticated ancestor of the root the response was
  built against.

The last of these is the "Merkle root in sigchain" idea from Keybase. A link
that cites epoch $E$ is signed evidence that the signer had seen a history
extending at least to $E$; a server that later wanted to rewind history
before $E$ would have to discard that link too, and any other client that has
read the chain would notice. Hostchain links carry a cited-root field of the
same shape, but the Rust hostchain verifier does not check it; for the host's
own chain the binding runs the other way, from the root to the tail.

## Revocation

A revocation is an ordinary link whose single member change assigns the
target device the role `NONE` with no keys and no metadata. The replay state
machine enforces the rules that make it meaningful:

- The signer must be an owner device that is currently active in the chain.
- Revoking *another* device must, in the same link, rotate every shared key
  at a role the revoked device could read; the new shared-key generations
  sign the link too, at the front of the stack. This is what ensures the
  revoked device cannot read anything encrypted afterward.
  [Chapter 5](05-generations.qmd) covers how the new generation is
  distributed.
- A device revoking *itself* carries no rotation. The roles it could read
  are marked stale, and a later link from another device must rotate them.
- The last owner device cannot be revoked.

Because a revocation is a link, it is placed in the tree, cited by later
links, and proven present like any other; a server cannot hide a revocation
from a client that loads the chain any more than it can hide a provisioning.

## Where to look

- `foks-proto`: `identity::chain` for `UserLink`, `UnsignedUserLink`,
  `ChangeMetadata`, and the signing-bytes construction; `host` for
  `HostchainLink` and `HostchainChange`; `identity::generic` for the
  subchain response.
- `foks-crypto`: `subchain_tree_location`, `commitment`, and the
  tree-location commitment.
- `foks-verify`: `user` (full and incremental chain verification),
  `user_transition` (the replay state machine), `team`, and `host`.
- `foks-client`: `team` for generic subchain verification.
- `foks-server`: `net::session` for cited-root and superseded-head checks;
  `services::generic` for subchain admission.
